card.hook: Picture a square so big and so bare that there isn't a single tree or flowerbed to photobomb you. That's Place Bellecour, and it's the easiest place in Lyon to get a clean, wide photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Bellecour, around the equestrian statue of Louis XIV at the centre. Face the statue and frame Fourvière hill behind it, so the red ground and the statue sit in front and the basilica rises behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the statue with Fourvière behind it. Switch to 0.5x for the whole open square and the line of façades. If your phone has zoom 2x, it pulls the basilica closer to the statue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the statue on one of the vertical lines, then tap the statue and slide the brightness down a touch so the sky and basilica keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. If the sun sits right behind the basilica, take a few steps to one side to dodge the glare.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Saint-Exupéry and Little Prince statue at the western end of the square. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the open square behind you. For a more relaxed shot, sit in one of the shaded deck chairs on the square.
card.ask_someone: Stand out on the open square, away from the statue, and ask your photographer to step back so Louis XIV and the Fourvière basilica fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Events and seasonal fittings like the ice rink can take up part of the square, so check the official site if you need a clear view. The statue may also be partly covered at times.
card.challenge: Take the same shot at 0.5x, 1x and 2x, then pick a winner and see if your travel buddy agrees.
card.good_to_know: The square measures 312 m by 200 m. The Louis XIV statue is by François-Frédéric Lemot and went up in 1825, after an earlier 1713 statue of the king was destroyed in 1793. The Saint-Exupéry and Little Prince statue at the west end arrived in 2000.

card.hook: Picture a calm lake, a long soft green line of trees and almost nothing else in the way. That's the big, relaxed view of Parc de la Tête d'Or, and it's easier to get than you'd think.
card.stand_here: Face back across the water so you see the park's tree line and the north shore behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole lake and the tree line in one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look. If your phone has zoom 2x or 5x, use it to pick out one patch of the far shore.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower line, so the horizon stays level and the trees fill the middle band.
card.best_time: Go early. Weekend afternoons get busy, and an early visit gives you cleaner shots with fewer people wandering through.
card.selfie_here: Try the small footbridge that leads out to the Île aux Cygnes. A wedding-photo guide calls it especially photogenic, with the lake and its reflections framing you nicely. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a little higher so the water and trees stay behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At the gilded iron gates at the Cité Internationale entrance, stand in front of the gate and ask a passer-by to step back and take your photo with the whole gate behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Access rules for the island itself may vary, and some greenhouse areas may not allow photos, so check the official site and the signs on the day.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the lake fills the bottom third and the trees make a neat green stripe across the middle. Bonus points if the horizon is perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: Parc de la Tête d'Or is Lyon's largest urban park, at about 117 hectares. It opened in 1857 on former Rhône floodplain and was laid out by the Swiss designers Bühler. It also holds the Jardin botanique de Lyon and a small free zoo, and boats go out on the lake in summer.

card.hook: Picture a whole row of pastel Renaissance facades lined up along the river, with a steep hill rising right behind them. That's Vieux Lyon from the middle of a footbridge, and it's hard to take a bad photo of it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of the Passerelle Saint-Vincent, the footbridge over the Saône. The subject is about 630 m to the south, so face Vieux Lyon with the old town to the south and the facades running along the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the line of facades with the hill behind. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want more sky and hill, and keep the horizon level so the buildings don't lean. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) is great for picking out rooflines and colours.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the facades, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: After dark is the showstopper, when the lights reflect on the water. Dusk is lovely too, because the sky still has some colour while the lights come on. At night, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the parapet or against your body to keep the lights sharp.
card.selfie_here: Head to Place Saint-Jean and stand on the square with the Cathédrale Saint-Jean-Baptiste facade behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and angle up so the facade fits over your shoulder. Zoom 0.5x helps if your phone has it. For a more typical old-town backdrop, try the steps of Montée du Change with the tall stone buildings behind you.
card.ask_someone: Try Quai Saint-Antoine on the Saône quay, after the Passerelle du Palais de Justice: hand your phone to a passer-by on the quay and stand so the old-town buildings and the cathedral area are behind you (check the exact spot when you get there).
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to public space, and please don't photograph inside residential courtyards or the traboules (the passages through buildings) without permission. The footbridge is narrow, so step to the side when you shoot so you don't block people.
card.challenge: Get the whole row of facades in one shot with a strip of river in front, then see if you can name your favourite pastel colour.
card.good_to_know: Vieux Lyon covers 24 hectares and is one of Europe's most extensive Renaissance neighbourhoods. It was the first site in France protected under the Malraux law in 1964, and it joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1998. It has three parts, Saint-Jean, Saint-Paul and Saint-Georges, each with its own character.

card.hook: Picture a giant cloud of stainless steel and glass that has landed right where two rivers meet. That's the Musée des Confluences, and from across the water it looks even better upside down in the Rhône.
card.stand_here: Stand on Berges du Rhône, the riverbank directly opposite the museum, which lies about 786 m to the south-west of it. Face south-west across the river and you'll see the museum reflected in the water, with the Raymond Barre footbridge at the edge of the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the museum, its reflection and the footbridge together. If you're close to the water and the building won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) gets you a tighter shot of the angular roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the water up with one of them, because a tilted horizon spoils a reflection.
card.best_time: Go at blue hour, just after sunset or before sunrise. The sky turns deep blue and the museum's lights show up in the water.
card.selfie_here: Try the garden steps of the museum, beneath the building's concrete arches. A French photo guide names them as a good backdrop for close-up photos of two people, so use the front camera and squeeze in together.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the riverbank facing the museum to take your photo, so the whole building fits in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are typically not allowed inside the museum, but that comes from a general travel page, so check the museum's official site first. The riverbank path is open to everyone, while the museum and its rooftop terrace are ticketed.
card.challenge: Get the museum in the top half, its reflection in the bottom half, and the footbridge peeking in at one edge, with the water line dead straight.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened on 20 December 2014 as a science centre and anthropology museum. It was designed by the Austrian firm Coop Himmelb(l)au in a deconstructivist style. It stands 44 m high, 150 m long and 83 m wide, so it's a big shape that fills a frame well.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Berges du Rhône, the riverbank directly opposite the museum, which lies about 786 m to the south-west of it. Face south-west across the river and you'll see the museum reflected in the water, with the Raymond Barre footbridge at the edge of the frame.

card.hook: Picture a bronze woman driving four wild horses across a square, with little water jets popping up from the paving around her. That's Place des Terreaux, and you can get a good photo here in about a minute.
card.stand_here: Start in the Jardin du musée des Beaux-Arts, in the museum grounds beside the square. The square's centre is about 1 minute on foot to the north. Face the museum's facade for your first shot.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x in the garden for the museum. Switch to zoom 0.5x out in the square to fit the fountain and the Hôtel de Ville together. Try zoom 2x or more (it depends on your phone) to pick out the horses of the chariot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the museum's facade with them so the walls stay straight, then tap the brightest part of the facade and slide it a touch darker so the pale stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon. The fountain area is busiest around midday, so those times are calmer for photos.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the centre of the Bartholdi Fountain with the Hôtel de Ville behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, hold the phone a bit higher and let the big building fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the square facing the Hôtel de Ville, while you pose by the fountain so City Hall is in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a busy square, so keep an eye on your pockets while you're snapping.
card.challenge: Take the same fountain shot twice, once at zoom 0.5x for the whole scene and once at zoom 2x or more for just the horses, then see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi made the fountain. It was first made for Bordeaux, but Lyon bought it in 1890 and unveiled it here on 22 September 1891. The Hôtel de Ville was built between 1646 and 1651 and rebuilt after a fire in 1674. The museum building began as a convent and became a museum in 1803.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start in the Jardin du musée des Beaux-Arts, in the museum grounds beside the square. The square's centre is about 1 minute on foot to the north. Face the museum's facade for your first shot.

card.hook: Walk into Place Saint-Jean and you'll do the same thing everyone does: tip your phone up, then up a bit more, because the square is snug and the cathedral is not small.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Saint-Jean, in front of the west façade, and face east so the Gothic front and its rose window fill your screen. Move between the corners of the square to change the angle without going anywhere.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the whole façade and the old Renaissance houses around it. Step back and use 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the rose window and the carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean backwards.
card.best_time: By day the sunlight picks out the carving on the front. The cathedral is also lit at twilight, which makes a good second visit, and in December the Festival of Lights puts a lighting display on the façade.
card.selfie_here: Take it on Place Saint-Jean, on the open square at the foot of the cathedral's front, with the façade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more of the building in, and keep the cathedral over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of Place Saint-Jean, opposite the cathedral, while you stand in front of the façade, so they can fit the whole front behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside, photos are for personal use only and no flash. Check the photo rules at the entrance and skip photographing worshippers during services. You may go through a security check with a bag check and metal detector.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole façade, then find the smallest carved detail you can spot and zoom in on it.
card.good_to_know: Work on the cathedral began in 1180 and finished in 1476. The west front is Gothic, while the apse and choir behind are Romanesque. It joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1998, and inside is a 14th-century astronomical clock.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place Saint-Jean, in front of the west façade, and face east so the Gothic front and its rose window fill your screen. Move between the corners of the square to change the angle without going anywhere.

card.hook: You're standing in a busy city square, looking at something that seems to be a grand old abbey. Surprise: it's one of the biggest art museums in France.
card.stand_here: Stand on Place des Terreaux, just north of the museum, and face south toward the main façade. The open square gives you room to step back and fit the whole front in one shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole façade across the square. Drop to 0.5x only if you have to stand close and the building won't fit. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for carved stonework, windows and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the building's vertical lines stay straight, then tap the façade and slide it a bit darker if the sky is washing out the stone.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, and late afternoon often gives softer light on the stone. Check how the shadows fall on the day.
card.selfie_here: Head into the museum garden (Jardin du Palais Saint-Pierre, reached from 20 Place des Terreaux) and stand near the arcades. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you want more in, and let the arches fill the background behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Hôtel de Ville forecourt and frame the square, while you stand on the square in front of the museum entrance. The entrance will land on the left of the shot and the Bartholdi fountain on the right.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum's guidance says to avoid selfie sticks inside. Flash is usually not allowed in the galleries, and personal photos without flash are generally fine, but check the signs, especially in temporary exhibitions.
card.challenge: Take one photo of the whole façade with the gridlines lined up, then one close-up of a single stone detail. See if a friend can guess where on the building it is.
card.good_to_know: The museum fills a former Benedictine convent, the Royal Abbey of Saint-Pierre-les-Nonnains, built in the 17th century and remodelled under Louis XIV. That's why the front looks more like an abbey than a gallery. The old cloister is now a quiet garden with statues, including two by Rodin. The museum was restored between 1988 and 1998 and stayed open to visitors the whole time.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Place des Terreaux, just north of the museum, and face south toward the main façade. The open square gives you room to step back and fit the whole front in one shot.

card.hook: You'll swear there's a staircase climbing between tall buildings, with neighbours leaning out of the windows. Then you realise it's all paint on the side of an ordinary apartment block. Lovely trick, and it's even better if you get the angle right.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Boulevard des Canuts and Rue Denfert-Rochereau, across the road and diagonally from the wall. The wall is to the south of you, so face it from there and the whole facade, staircase and painted street life fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which gives the most natural look to the painted staircase. If the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole wall, switch to 0.5x and keep the wall's edges parallel to the sides of your screen so the buildings don't lean. For a close-up of a window or a figure, try 2x if your phone has it.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the wall, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright, so the painted colours stay rich and the staircase keeps its shading.
card.best_time: Go in the morning if you can. Guides say midday sun flattens the painted staircase, and then the 3D magic fades.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement of Boulevard des Canuts with the painted central staircase behind you. It's the part of the wall guides say draws the most cameras, so it gives you the strongest illusion behind your head. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more wall in, and keep the staircase over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the opposite side of Boulevard des Canuts while you stand in front of the mural, so they can fit you and the whole wall into one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep clear of the doorways and watch the traffic on the boulevard while you line up your shot. If you walk up the hill instead of taking Metro Line C to Hénon, wear shoes that cope with the steep slopes.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the whole wall, then hunt for a painted window or figure and get a close-up, as if you'd caught a neighbour peeking out.
card.good_to_know: The Mur des Canuts is a huge painted wall that looks like a real street scene. Guides say it was repainted in 1987, 1997 and 2013, so details may differ from older photos you've seen. It sits on the side of an ordinary residential building, so please keep the doorways clear.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Boulevard des Canuts and Rue Denfert-Rochereau, across the road and diagonally from the wall. The wall is to the south of you, so face it from there and the whole facade, staircase and painted street life fit in one frame.

card.hook: Picture a grand 19th-century opera house wearing a modern glass hat. That's the Opéra de Lyon, and it looks a bit like two buildings that have agreed to share a roof.
card.stand_here: Stand out in Place de la Comédie, in front of the main façade, and face the opera. The Hôtel de Ville is across the square behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the arcades, the muse statues and a slice of the square into one shot. Then try 1x for a calmer look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the statues and the glass vault.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the columns up with the vertical lines so they don't lean, and leave a little space around the building so you can crop afterwards.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or dusk, when the statues and arcades are lit up. As the light fades, switch on night mode and keep your elbows tucked in or lean on a railing.
card.selfie_here: Take it on Place de la Comédie, right in front of the Opéra's arcaded front. Use the front camera, switch to a wider view if your phone has one, and turn so the eight muse statues sit over your shoulder. Dusk is the time one guide recommends.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Place Louis-Pradel end of the square with their back to the Hôtel de Ville side, then pose in front of the opera so they can fit the whole building in.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open and free to photograph from. If you go inside for a show, flash and recording are not allowed during performances.
card.challenge: Count all eight muses along the top, then see if you can fit every one of them into your selfie.
card.good_to_know: The first opera house in Lyon, the Grand Théâtre, opened in 1756 and was designed by Jacques-Germain Soufflot. The present building opened on 1 July 1831. Between 1985 and 1993, architect Jean Nouvel rebuilt the inside, keeping only the foyer and the outer façade, digging down for rehearsal space and doubling the height with the glass vault.

card.hook: Locals call this hilltop church "the upside-down elephant", and once you spot the four tower 'legs' sticking up, you can't unsee it. Lyon's white basilica looks down on the old town like it owns the place.
card.stand_here: Head for Place Saint-Jean in Vieux Lyon, the old-town square at the foot of the hill. Face up the hill to the north-west, where the basilica rises above the old rooftops and facades.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the basilica and the rooftops sit together in one frame. If the church looks small, try 2x. Keep 0.5x for the old facades in the square, because it makes the basilica tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the basilica, then slide the brightness down a little so the white stone keeps its detail against the sky.
card.best_time: Check the sky before you go, because a clear day suits the white stone best.
card.selfie_here: Walk up to the terrace in front of the basilica (the esplanade on Fourvière hill) and face out over the city, so the church is behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little high so you both fit in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Place Saint-Jean, near the Cathédrale Saint-Jean-Baptiste, to shoot up toward the hilltop so the whole basilica fits, while you stand a few steps in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos without flash are allowed inside the basilica, but be discreet and respect prayer times and celebrations. Selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the church.
card.challenge: Find all four tower 'legs' of the upside-down elephant and get every one in your shot.
card.good_to_know: The basilica was built between 1872 and 1896, on ground that was once the Roman forum of Trajan. Architect Pierre Bossan mixed Romanesque and Byzantine styles, and the bell tower is topped with a gilded statue of the Virgin Mary. It's a place of worship with guided tours and a museum, and the north tower is only open at certain times, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Place Saint-Jean in Vieux Lyon, the old-town square at the foot of the hill. Face up the hill to the north-west, where the basilica rises above the old rooftops and facades.

card.hook: Lyon's city hall is so wide and so tidy that it almost looks like a stage set, with a pavilion at each end and a fountain parked right in front. Even if your photo is mostly about proving you were here, this is an easy win.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place des Terreaux, by the Bartholdi Fountain, and face the Hôtel de Ville. If you're coming by metro, get off at Hôtel de Ville on line A, and it's about 2 minutes on foot to the east, with the façade facing you across the square.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the fountain and the whole façade in one shot. Use 1x for a more natural look. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the clock tower and the horseback carving in the middle of the façade.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the façade up with them, so the building stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Come at dusk or in the evening, when the building is lit up and glowing. In the dark, hold your phone with both hands and use night mode.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Bartholdi Fountain in the middle of Place des Terreaux with the Hôtel de Ville behind you, and use the front camera. If your phone has a 0.5x button on the front, tap it so more of the building fits over your shoulder. Dusk is the best light.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand across the square while you stand by the fountain, so the whole façade fits in the shot instead of just a slice of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The inside isn't normally open to visitors, so plan on photographing from outside.
card.challenge: Find the king on horseback in the middle of the façade, zoom in on him, and then get a second shot with you pointing at him.
card.good_to_know: Building work began on 5 September 1646, timed to King Louis XIV's birthday, and the council first met here in 1652. A fire in 1674 led to the façade being restored and altered. The belfry was added to the UNESCO World Heritage group of Belfries of Belgium and France in 2005.

card.hook: Twelve streets pour into this square, so there's always someone crossing your shot. Don't fight it. The white marble fountain in the middle is big enough to win.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place des Jacobins, in front of the fountain, near the centre of the square. The middle of the square lies just to the west. Face the white marble Fontaine des Jacobins so the 19th-century facades fill in behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the fountain with the facades behind it. Drop to 0.5x for the basin and the buildings all around, then try 2x or 5x for the statues and carvings (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white stonework, then slide it a little darker so the marble keeps its detail instead of turning plain white.
card.best_time: Golden hour or evening is the favourite, when the fountain and buildings are lit. Early morning is quieter and shows off the carvings, though the light varies, so check on the day.
card.selfie_here: Head for the spot directly in front of the Fontaine des Jacobins, at the centre of the square. Use the front camera, turn so the fountain is over your shoulder, and use the wide setting if your phone has one so the facades fit in too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at a diagonal near Rue Émile Zola, with you beside the fountain, so the basin sits in the foreground and the square's facades are behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square can be crowded at peak times and on market days, so watch for traffic and passers-by at the edges of your frame.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 5x and find all four statues on top of the fountain. Bonus points if you can say which one is Flandrin.
card.good_to_know: The square dates back to 1556 and is named after the Dominican friars, known as Jacobins, who had a convent here from 1296. The fountain you see now was inaugurated on 14 July 1885 and designed by Gaspard André. Its four statues show the artists Flandrin, Audran, Coustou and Philibert de l'Orme.

card.hook: Two thousand years ago around 10,000 people squeezed onto these stone steps, and you get the same view with far better legroom. Lyon sprawls out behind the curve like a modern backdrop to an ancient show.
card.stand_here: Climb the seating at the Théâtre antique de Fourvière to the upper tiers, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face down over the big curve of stone, with the city of Lyon spread out behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole sweep of seating and the city in one go. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, and 2x for close-ups of the stone steps or a single row.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, tuck the curved rows along the lower third of the frame, and tap the sky then slide it a touch darker so the stone keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour, when the low light warms the stone and the city behind it.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the stage floor of the Grand Théâtre and turn your back on the stage. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the stone tiers rise up behind you in one big curve.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the top rows by the metal railing and shoot down over the whole theatre while you stand on the stage or the lower tiers.
card.rules_and_safety: The stone steps can be uneven and slippery, especially after rain, so wear shoes with good grip. The museum terrace nearby may need museum access, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Find the curved rows of stone and line up a shot where they lead the eye straight to the centre, like a giant arrow.
card.good_to_know: The first theatre went up around 15 BC, and in the early 2nd century it was enlarged to about 108 m across, with room for some 10,000 people. It's part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for the historic centre of Lyon. It's still in use today, and the Nuits de Fourvière festival is held here every year.

card.hook: Most spots give you one picture. This market gives you a new one every few steps: a glass building outside, then counters, dishes and people in motion inside.
card.stand_here: The phone icon sits right at the Halles de Lyon-Paul Bocuse, so once you arrive you're already in position. Take your first shot of the building from here, then walk around it and head inside.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the building and for stalls at normal distance. Go to 0.5x inside to fit in the whole hall, and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details across a counter.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's straight edges with them, so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Opening hours can change, so check the official site before you go. Pick a time that suits you, and be ready to wait a moment for a clear view of a stall.

card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole hall, then find three close-ups of a single stall or dish. Bonus points if a passer-by wanders into the frame at just the right moment.
card.good_to_know: The Halles de Lyon-Paul Bocuse is a covered food market in Lyon. A mural honouring Paul Bocuse sits directly across Cours Lafayette from it. Check the mural's street number on site, as the pages we found disagree.

card.hook: Four wild horses are rearing out of the water, and the woman driving them looks completely calm about it. It's hard to take a boring photo of the Fontaine Bartholdi.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place des Terreaux, in front of the fountain. It's directly north of you, so you'll be facing it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole chariot and all four horses. If the fountain won't fit, or you want the tall buildings around the square in the shot, tap 0.5x. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is great for the horses' heads and the spray.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the horses, then slide the brightness down a little so the bright spray and sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the day and you'll usually get fewer people in front of the fountain. In the evening it's lit up and has a totally different mood, so try both if you can.
card.selfie_here: Use the square itself, Place des Terreaux, next to the fountain and the City Hall. Switch to the front camera, tap 0.5x and put the fountain over your shoulder. There's no perfect spot, so test the angle when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Try asking a passer-by to shoot from the sides of the square while you stand with the fountain behind you, so they can fit in the whole thing.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public square and free to see. Works have sometimes put up fencing or scaffolding, or left the basin empty, so check current conditions before you go.
card.challenge: Count the four horses, then find the reins, which are made of water weeds, and get them in your shot.
card.good_to_know: Bartholdi, the sculptor of the Statue of Liberty, designed this fountain. The four horses stand for four great rivers of France. It's actually lead on an iron frame and weighs about 21 tons. It was built in 1889 and put up on this square in September 1892, and it re-opened in March 2018 after restoration.

card.hook: This church looks like it's ready for a siege, with thick walls, narrow slit windows and a watchtower. It's a surprisingly sturdy sight in the middle of a calm Lyon neighbourhood.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rue Claude Bourgelat, the street beside the basilica, and face east, because the church is to the east of you. You get the whole building sitting among its neighbours, which feels like Lyon rather than a postcard.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural street view. If the street feels too narrow to fit the whole church, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tower and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the church's straight vertical edges with them, so the walls and tower don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to old pale stone. Go early and you'll usually get fewer people and cars in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the paved square in front of the church on Place d'Ainay and stand with the pale stone façade behind you. For a closer shot, stand in front of the pointed-arch main portal with it right behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more church, and let the building rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Rue Bourgelat facing the church, since the basilica sits at the end of that street and they can frame the whole thing from there.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is still used for worship, so be considerate if anything is going on. Ask or check before photographing inside.
card.challenge: Find the watchtower, zoom in on it, and get it standing perfectly straight against your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The abbey church was built at the end of the 11th century and consecrated on 29 January 1107. It became a basilica in 1905. It sits in Lyon's UNESCO-listed historic centre and is 37 metres long, with a nave 17 metres wide.

card.hook: You'll walk into a dark little arched passage off a Lyon street and come out into a courtyard with a stone stairway six floors tall. It's a proper "wait, what?" moment.
card.stand_here: Stand on rue Imbert-Colomès, at the traboule entrance (no. 29), and face the arched passage so it frames the way into the courtyard. It's a less obvious approach than the Place Colbert door, so you get a different view of the entrance.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x at the entrance to catch the arch. Once you're inside, switch to zoom 0.5x so the whole tall stairwell fits in one frame, and hold the phone level so the lines don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the arch up with the vertical lines, then tap the bright part of the courtyard and slide it a touch darker so the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when you get the most light inside the court. Opening hours aren't confirmed, so check access locally before you plan around a particular time.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the stone steps inside the courtyard, with the stairwell rising behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the big staircase fill the background over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: People live here, so keep your voice low, don't block the doors and don't photograph residents. One guide says photography is generally allowed, but opening hours and photo restrictions aren't confirmed, so check access locally.
card.challenge: Shoot the arch from the street, then find the same lines repeating in the railings and landings inside. Can you get three frames that all feel like one story?
card.good_to_know: The building dates from 1840 and is a good example of the canuts' architecture. The canuts were the silk weavers who shaped this neighbourhood. The name comes from the Voraces, weavers known for their republican uprisings of 1848 and 1849. Today it's social housing, and the court and its two staircases are classified as a historic monument.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on rue Imbert-Colomès, at the traboule entrance (no. 29), and face the arched passage so it frames the way into the courtyard. It's a less obvious approach than the Place Colbert door, so you get a different view of the entrance.

card.hook: From up on the hill, Lyon's tallest building looks like a tiny dark tower poking out of a sea of red rooftops. That's the charm. Treat it as part of the skyline, not a star on its own.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Esplanade de Fourvière, the hilltop terrace above Vieux Lyon. It's on the hill about 2 km to the west of the tower. Face the tower, with the red rooftops of Vieux Lyon below it.
card.zoom: Zoom 5x for the tower itself (higher zooms depend on your phone). Then drop to zoom 1x or 0.5x for the wide city view.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the tower on a vertical line, then tap the tower and drag the brightness slider a little darker so the sky stays deep and the city lights don't blow out.
card.best_time: Come at blue hour, just after sunset, when the city lights come on against the dark sky. Use night mode and brace your elbows on the terrace wall so you stay steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Esplanade of Fourvière at the viewpoint over Old Lyon. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and turn so the tower is behind your shoulder. For sunset, the Jardin des Chartreux terrace near Place Rouville is another candidate, with the tower behind you. We haven't tested either one, so check the framing on the spot.
card.rules_and_safety: The esplanade is an open public terrace and free to visit. The tower is an office building, so this is a photo to take from a distance.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the very top and see if you can catch the lights glowing blue or mauve, then you've photographed tomorrow's air quality.
card.good_to_know: Tour Incity is 200 m tall with 39 floors, the tallest building in the Greater Lyon area. It was built between 2013 and 2015 in the La Part-Dieu business district, on the site of the old UAP tower. Its top is shaped to look symmetrical from wherever you see it in the city, and the summit lights shade from blue to mauve to show the next day's air quality.

card.hook: Spot the Eiffel Tower's little cousin standing right beside a pale white basilica, with all of Lyon spread out below it. It's a strange pair, and that's why it makes such a good photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Esplanade de la Basilique Notre-Dame de Fourvière, in front of the basilica. Face north and look towards the tower: it's a short distance to the north and rises behind and beside the church, with the skyline below.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the tower, the basilica and the skyline in one shot. Try 0.5x if the esplanade is crowded or you want more of the basilica. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) gets you in close on the lattice against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the mast up with a vertical line so the tower stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Sunset is lovely, when the sky and skyline colour up behind the tower. During the Fête des Lumières the tower is lit up, which makes for striking evening shots.
card.selfie_here: Use the esplanade in front of the basilica, with the tower in the frame above the city. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the tower over your shoulder. For a different look, try a viewpoint terrace on the Parc des Hauteurs paths, where the tower peeks through the trees behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Quai des Célestins, between Pont Bonaparte and Passerelle du Palais-de-Justice, to photograph you with the hill behind, so the basilica and tower both appear in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower is closed to visitors and its base is fenced off, so every photo is taken from outside. Check the official site before you go for any event or restriction.
card.challenge: Get the mast perfectly upright on a grid line, with a little sky left above its tip. No stray people or railings creeping in at the edges!
card.good_to_know: The tower was built between 1892 and 1894, three years after the Eiffel Tower. It's 101 m tall (about 86 m before the television antenna was added) and weighs 210 tons. It sits at 372 metres above sea level, the highest point in Lyon. It was once an observation tower, but it's been closed to visitors since 1953 and now works as a television mast.
